claims.headline: Task-specialised open model beats Jev on rewriting, trails on routing

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.05107
claims.claim_text: In BrowseComp-Plus, dual-system agents that let SearchJev take confident short decisions cut median active search time 3.7–4.7-fold and output tokens 3.3–4.8-fold against a System-2-only agent while raising answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%; against a Jev 1.13 agent the 0.8B model used fewer calls and less time at the same accuracy.
limitations: One deep-research benchmark.
claims.headline: Search agent: 3.7–4.7× faster, accuracy 45% → 54%

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.06354
claims.claim_text: Jev answered every adjacency query correctly and performed relatively well on cycle, connectivity and distance judgments, but reached only 67.80% on exact degree and 61.25% on articulation points, so recognising an explicitly listed edge did not establish neighbour counting or connectivity reasoning.
limitations: Small graphs.
claims.headline: Reads every edge; counts degree right 68% of the time

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.06625
claims.claim_text: Across seven political-science replications, Jev matched or came close to GPT-6 Luna and Qwen3.8-27B against human coding, but had no cost advantage over GPT-6 Luna at OpenAI’s batch prices: it bills the question and every option as input, 1.2–3.3 times as many input tokens per decision as Luna, which wrote about four output tokens per answer.
claims.metric: input tokens billed relative to GPT-6 Luna
limitations: Prices at the time of study.
claims.headline: Same accuracy, no cost advantage at batch prices

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.06625
claims.claim_text: When each question was asked once, Jev’s probabilities were better calibrated than GPT-6 Luna’s token probabilities but not consistently better than those of the open-weight Qwen3.8-27B.
limitations: Human coding as the benchmark.
claims.headline: Better calibrated than a commercial LLM, not than an open one

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.06744
claims.claim_text: A head that scores each option blind to the others made the 182M-parameter Turkish model order-invariant by construction, whereas a sequential head trained with shuffled options changed 2.3–2.8% of its answers when only the option order changed; the released model answers in a median 102.5 ms on one CPU thread.
limitations: Same author built the benchmark; results not blind.
claims.headline: Order invariance by construction; sequential heads still flip 2–3%

claims.subject: src:typesafe-evals
claims.claim_text: The vendor’s workflow-evals dashboard averages four structured workflows (security incidents, agent-trace observability, invoice processing, customer service) against reference labels averaged from GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 at high thinking. In workflow mode it lists Jev at 67.8% mean agreement for $0.0004 and 0.4 s per case, against 74.1% for the best listed configuration (“sol”, $0.0836, 23.3 s) and 73.1% for Opus 5; every listed model scored higher in workflow mode than as a single prompt.
claims.metric: mean agreement with reference labels (workflow mode)
limitations: Reference labels are frontier-model answers, not human gold.
Workflows written by the vendor.
claims.headline: Vendor dashboard: 67.8% agreement at $0.0004 and 0.4 s per case

claims.subject: gh:anessbelbati/jev-rerank-bench
claims.claim_text: Asked to rate thirty search results in one call, Jev’s four-level rubric scored nDCG@10 0.692 against 0.691 for Cohere Rerank 4 Pro when each dataset counts once (0.738 vs 0.756 when each question counts once) at 422 ms against 844 ms per query; on NevIR negation pairs Jev got 71% right against 67%.
limitations: Weighting questions equally puts Cohere ahead.
claims.headline: Reranking: ties Cohere Rerank 4 Pro at half the latency

claims.subject: gh:bitnovus/jev-spam-eval
claims.claim_text: With written category definitions and no labelled examples, Jev reached 98.64% accuracy on a 5,733-email ham/spam/phishing test against 98.87% for TF-IDF logistic regression trained on about 4,600 labelled messages per fold; on 853 recent phishing messages, Jev with enriched email context caught 95.31% against 75.26% for regression on the same evidence.
limitations: Phishing recall comparison uses enriched context for both.
claims.headline: Zero-shot spam: matches a trained baseline; catches more new phishing

claims.subject: gh:coldteadotai/abide
claims.claim_text: Replaying 93 coding-agent sessions (1,256 edits, 147 turns) against the projects’ own rules, Jev flagged 39 edits and 15 turns as rule violations; an independent reviewer confirmed 10 of the edits and 11 of the turns.
claims.metric: flagged edits confirmed by a reviewer
limitations: Two repositories; one reviewer.
claims.headline: Rule checks on agent edits: 10 of 39 flags confirmed

claims.subject: gh:gaurav-gosain/jev-sec-bench
claims.claim_text: Run once against jev-1.13.0 without threshold tuning, Jev classified all 662 labelled messages of deepset/prompt-injections with 96.5% accuracy (F1 95.6%), and scored the vulnerable half above its secure twin in 178 of 200 matched code pairs (89.0%).
limitations: Public corpora; possible training overlap unknown.
claims.headline: Blind security run: 96.5% on prompt injection, 89% on code pairs

claims.subject: gh:gautamtalksdev/jevbench
claims.claim_text: In a preregistered ChaosNLI study, Jev’s Choice probabilities were close to calibrated where annotators agreed but overconfident where they split (mean confidence 0.81 against 0.47 annotator agreement; bias-corrected ΔECE 0.264); normalised Noul probabilities degraded less (ΔECE 0.076).
limitations: One dataset; Choice and Noul arms differ.
claims.headline: Overconfident where 100 annotators disagree (0.81 vs 0.47)

claims.subject: gh:jevals/jevals-data
claims.claim_text: In the 2026-09-18 release scored against human labels, Jev tied Gemini 3.8 Flash for first in Decision Score on PubMedQA yes/no questions (69.0 vs 73.0) at $0.029 per 1,000 decisions, tied for second of eight on Banking77 intents (67.8 vs 74.1), and like every model did not clearly beat guessing on HelpSteer2 helpfulness.
claims.metric: Decision Score on PubMedQA (100 = perfect, 0 = base-rate guessing)
limitations: Three tasks; leaderboard ranks use interval ties.
claims.headline: Independent boards: top tier on yes/no, second on intents, no model beats guessing on helpfulness

claims.subject: gh:lexmount/webjev
claims.claim_text: Driving the same jev-ultrafast browser agent on 125 real-website tasks graded by deterministic verifiers, WebJev-35B-A3B completed 38.52% and Jev 1.13 16.67%, although on eight single-step decision benchmarks the two were close (83.72% vs 84.70%).
limitations: Authors’ task suite; their own model is the comparator.
claims.headline: Browser tasks: specialised open model 38.5% vs Jev 16.7%; single steps alike

claims.subject: gh:nanmicoder/jev-arena
claims.claim_text: On 10,000 comments re-labelled by GPT-6 Astra, Jev 1.13 finished in 203.2 s for $0.84 against 823.5 s and an estimated $1.50 for DeepSeek Flash, with lower agreement on all three labels (all three right: 62.69% vs 67.26%).
claims.metric: all three labels agree with the reference
limitations: Reference labels from another model, not human gold.
claims.headline: 10,000 comments: 4× faster than a chat model, five points less agreement

claims.subject: gh:realzachi/pg-jev
claims.claim_text: Packing rows into one Jev request, where Jev must find each row by its position in an array, the author found batches of 1–20 rows judged 100% correctly against ground truth on three conditions over 400-row tables, batches of 40 at 92–98% and batches of 80 at 77–94%; batches of 20 cost 4% more tokens than batches of 40 at about the same latency.
claims.metric: rows judged correctly in batches of 80
limitations: Three structured conditions; author-run.
claims.headline: More rows per request, fewer correct: 100% → 77–94%

claims.subject: gh:shimo4228/jev-skill-router
claims.claim_text: Run for a week as a Claude Code skill router, Jev’s suggestion was followed by a call of the suggested skill in 28 of 539 cases; the author removed it because the log could not separate Jev’s picks from the agent’s own choices.
claims.metric: suggestions followed by the suggested skill
claims.task: Skill routing in a coding agent
limitations: One user’s week of sessions.
claims.headline: A week as a skill router: 28 of 539 suggestions used, then removed

claims.subject: gh:suenot/codex-jev-router
claims.claim_text: In the author’s four-arm benchmark, Codex subagents whose model was chosen by Jev were 27.2% cheaper than fixed high-effort subagents yet 69.7% more expensive than a single extra-high-effort agent, and the router was withdrawn.
claims.metric: cost relative to a single extra-high-effort agent
limitations: Author-run tasks; the comparison depends on the baseline chosen.
claims.headline: Routing subagents with Jev: cheaper than one baseline, dearer than another

claims.subject: gh:uspraveen/jevify
claims.claim_text: On the author’s jev-bench, Jev 1.13.0 reached 0.733 accuracy with ECE 0.113 — calibrated on crisp questions, overconfident where people disagree — while a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B readout with a coherence objective reached 0.763 accuracy, ECE 0.056 and a distance to the human label distribution of 0.301 against Jev’s 0.432.
limitations: The author built the benchmark and the winning model.
claims.headline: Open 9B readout edges Jev on accuracy and calibration in the author’s benchmark

claims.subject: gh:wondertwins/jev-benchmark
claims.claim_text: Choosing chess moves, jev-1.13.0 was no better than random from a raw board (mean centipawn loss 533 from a FEN string against 403 for random moves) but fell to 144 with code-computed facts; with one-ply tactical facts it found mate-in-one 24% of the time and played at roughly 950 Elo.
claims.metric: mean centipawn loss with code-computed facts
limitations: Single author; one engine-anchored ladder.
claims.headline: Chess: random from the raw board, competent once code supplies the facts

claims.subject: gh:yinsongxu/llm2jev
claims.claim_text: On the 231 public JevBench items, LLM2Jev on a local Qwen3.5-4B reached 76.2% accuracy with a median latency of 48 ms (P95 346 ms), against 652 ms (P95 722 ms) for hosted Jev 1.13.0.
limitations: Hosted latency includes the network; local runs do not.
claims.headline: Local 4B readout: 76% on public JevBench at 48 ms

claims.subject: gh:zhuyansen/jev-search-rerank-eval
claims.claim_text: Reranking an embedding ranker’s top 30 with Jev changed NDCG@10 by +0.053 under Jev-made labels, +0.012 under merged labels and −0.028 under labels from an unrelated model, while fusing Jev with the embedding ranking gained +0.090 and survived removing Jev from the judging.
claims.metric: NDCG@10 change from Jev reranking (unrelated-model labels)
limitations: One catalogue; graded labels from model judges.
claims.headline: Grading Jev with Jev’s own labels inflates its gain

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.03387
claims.claim_text: With 80 calibration pairs per source task, none-score rejection policies exceeded 5% target false rejection in six of twelve task transfers for each of Laya and Jev; a Jev policy calibrated on DBpedia rejected 69.3% of covered Emotion test inputs, and an Emotion-calibrated Jev policy disabled rejection entirely until it was recalibrated on target labels.
claims.metric: false rejection of covered inputs after transfer (DBpedia → Emotion)
limitations: Two ordinary candidates and natural names in the transfer matrix.
claims.headline: Rejection thresholds do not travel: 69% false rejection after transfer

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.03387
claims.claim_text: On CLINC150 with BM25-retrieved menus, raising the candidate count from two to ten raised Laya’s out-of-scope detection from 83.0% to 99.0% and its false rejection of covered queries from 15.2% to 48.8%, while Jev kept false rejection near 3% but its out-of-scope detection fell from 84.0% to 75.0% (Qwen2.5-7B: 85.0% to 63.0%); with artificial omission at five candidates, Jev detected 63.7% of missing answers.
claims.metric: out-of-scope detection with ten retrieved candidates
limitations: Natural-miss estimates at ten candidates rest on five cases.
claims.headline: More candidates: Laya rejects half of covered queries, Jev misses a quarter of out-of-scope ones

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07953
claims.claim_text: With the complete rule inventory held fixed, adding five retrieved precedents raised Jev’s exact-match moderation accuracy by 12.35 points on six large PluRule communities, 5.20 points on the PluRule test intersection and 22.20 points on HateModerate, while Laya changed by −1.4 to +1.4 points on PluRule; with Noul questions, precedents raised Jev’s AUROC on OLID from .789 to .816 but lowered Laya’s from .800 to .702.
limitations: Matched contrasts on public benchmarks; generative LLMs not run under the same conditions.
claims.headline: Precedents help Jev pick the right rule (+5 to +22 points); Laya barely moves

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07953
claims.claim_text: Jev’s Choice confidence ranked its own errors with correctness AUC .628–.823 across five benchmarks; at confidence ≥ 0.8 it kept 45.0% of six-community PluRule decisions at 79.5% accuracy (65.1% overall) and 71.9% of ModerationBench decisions at 94.3% accuracy (86.7% overall), whereas Laya’s confidence ranked errors at AUC .560–.593 and covered 2.0–19.2% of decisions at that threshold.
limitations: The authors note that confidence is not consistently calibrated.
claims.headline: Jev confidence supports selective review; Laya’s barely ranks errors

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07716
claims.claim_text: Across 91 menu-only interventions on seven open decision-model families, restricting the cached first-pass distribution to the new menu predicted post-intervention accuracy within 4.2 points (exactly for the Open-Jev family), whereas the same estimator erred by 1.6–15.8 points on same-scale generative models and a probability-level variant erred by 21.0 points.
claims.metric: maximum prediction error for menu-only interventions
limitations: Open models only.
claims.headline: Menu changes are predictable offline for decision models, not for generative LLMs

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07716
claims.claim_text: Averaging sixteen order-permuted passes lowered expected calibration error by 67% but changed accuracy by at most 3.83 points (pooled +1.2); escalating the least-confident items from Kev-0.8B to larger siblings reached the 9B model’s single-pass accuracy at 1.0–6.3 forward units instead of 11, and on CLINC150 a 0.8B model on a curated five-candidate menu reached 95.4% against 80.0% for a 4B model on the full 150-label menu.
claims.metric: CLINC150 accuracy, 0.8B model on a curated five-candidate menu
limitations: Compute measured in forward units of the smallest model.
claims.headline: Extra passes buy calibration, not accuracy; escalate and curate instead

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07730
claims.claim_text: On 10,027 test decisions from 59 sources, applying the same layers eight times raised accuracy from 58.4% (a non-looped model of the same shape, data and recipe) to 72.0% at 7.7 times the computation; calibration error was lowest after three loops and rose again as confidence kept increasing on wrong answers, while detection of missing evidence improved (AUROC 0.835 → 0.935) and hard answers on evidence-removed items fell from 27.1% to 17.5%.
limitations: Three training seeds; differences of one or two points on small groups need their intervals.
claims.headline: Looping a small decision model: +13.5 points at 7.7× compute

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07730
claims.claim_text: Queried as a reference, hosted Jev (jev-1.13.0) answered 78.9% of the 10,027 test decisions correctly but gave a hard answer to 62.8% of 382 items whose deciding evidence had been removed (evidence AUROC 0.743); on liar chains its accuracy fell from 100% at one step to 62.5% at three and stayed near chance from six steps on, while its confidence stayed above its accuracy.
limitations: Single runs of the hosted model; not trained on the authors’ data.
claims.headline: Hosted Jev answers 63% of evidence-removed items and loses track after three steps

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.08089
claims.claim_text: In synthetic simulations, plans for the same semantic join differed by up to three orders of magnitude in cost; bands calibrated on each plan’s own candidates made selection pushdown meet the output target on 62% of instances against 96% for pull-up, per-tuple prices met an output-level target at 7,164 cost units against 37,256 for the cheapest operator-level band, and an overconfident decision model predicted output precision 0.981 where 0.872 was realised.
claims.metric: cost of meeting an output target with per-tuple prices
limitations: Synthetic workload designed to make each effect visible.
claims.headline: Calibrated confidence prices query plans; overconfidence hides output errors

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07327
claims.claim_text: In Adaptive PickPlace, exposing only the active behaviour-tree node’s fields raised correct joint skill–object decisions from 90/120 (all fields exposed) to 113/120 and closed-loop four-object completion from 0/30 to 18/30, at 128 ms against 316 ms per decision; with model scores held fixed, removing stage gating or the external postcondition let the agent act out of order or stop early in 10 of 15 saved states.
limitations: Saved states repeat across seeds; counts are descriptive.
claims.headline: Node-local candidates: 113/120 correct decisions against 90/120

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07327
claims.claim_text: With an explicit ABSTAIN candidate, complete-candidate scoring rejected 28 of 30 menus that contained no valid action but chose the correct action in only 17 of 30 valid menus (45/60 overall against 51/60 for autoregressive generation), and changing only the candidate order changed the selected value in 46 of 120 node-local states.
claims.metric: correct decisions on valid menus with ABSTAIN offered
claims.task: Rejection when no candidate is valid
limitations: 60 held-out cases; one open model.
claims.headline: ABSTAIN catches invalid menus but costs valid answers; order flips 46 of 120 picks

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07177
claims.claim_text: Zero-shot, the open contrastive decision model CLM-v0.1-8B scored 0.351–0.593 as a judge, statistically indistinguishable from chance on RM-Bench and JudgeBench and one constant label on HaluEval, while a same-size reward model reached 0.764–0.976 and a generative judge 0.611–0.778; its decisions flipped under answer-order swap at 0.0002 against 0.2188 for the generative judge.
limitations: One open checkpoint, zero-shot; fine-tuned heads moved accuracy by −0.028 to +0.060.
claims.headline: Open contrastive decision model judges near chance, but ignores answer order

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07177
claims.claim_text: Raw CLM confidences were overconfident by +0.235 to +0.401; one pooled temperature fitted on held-out calibration items brought ECE to 0.032–0.062, but at a preregistered 0.97 retention bar the confidence-gated cascade escalated 92.3–100% of items to the strong judge, because calibrated confidence about a near-chance judge leaves almost nothing to keep.
claims.metric: escalation fraction at the 0.97 retention bar (minimum)
limitations: The strong judge is a hosted service whose configuration can change.
claims.headline: Calibrated after one temperature, yet the gate escalates 92–100%

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07019
claims.claim_text: On Evidence Inference 2.0’s test split (1,218 prompts in 333 articles), the 4B model met four criteria registered on OSF before its test predictions: ECE 0.0168 against a limit of 0.05, log loss 0.8603 below the prior and 0.1829 below Gemma 4 31B-it reading the same input, and macro-F1 0.9248 against 0.8668.
limitations: Public test labels; pre-training overlap of both models is unknown.
claims.headline: Registered test passed: ECE 0.017, macro-F1 0.92 against 0.87 for a 31B model

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.07019
claims.claim_text: Reading checks showed what the answers rest on: with no article macro-F1 fell to 0.4384, the title alone added 0.0939, and exchanging intervention and comparator reversed only 66.5% of direction answers; handing the least confident 10% of answers to Gemma 4 31B-it gave 0.9335 against 0.9269 alone, with no difference claimed.
claims.metric: direction answers reversed after exchanging the arms
limitations: Descriptive checks.
claims.headline: Swap the two arms and a third of answers keep their direction

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.06985
claims.claim_text: Calibrated on a random 5% slice, one unrelaxed forward pass decided crystal stability better than each potential’s recalibrated relax-and-threshold practice for MACE-MP-0 (log-loss 0.191 against 0.247) and CHGNet (0.196 against 0.266) at about a thirtieth of the cost, and slightly worse for four newer potentials (log-loss higher by 0.009–0.033).
limitations: Benchmark labels are DFT energies on a fixed hull.
claims.headline: One calibrated pass against a relaxation: as good or better at a thirtieth of the cost

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.06985
claims.claim_text: In a registered prospective test on newly computed candidates, 23 of 397 labelled test candidates (5.8%) proved stable; single-pass forecasts calibrated only on existing data over-stated that fraction by 0.8–2.1 percentage points across six backbones and ranked candidates with AUROC 0.965–0.982 (intervals and AUROC were not registered).
limitations: Candidates generated by substitution; DFT labels aligned to MP by fixed corrections.
claims.headline: Registered prospective test: stable fraction forecast within 2.1 points

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.08155
claims.claim_text: Across six benchmarks S1-MAS reached the highest mean accuracy (macro-average 93.97%) while using 78.3–94.0% fewer GPT-4o tokens and 58.2–91.7% lower latency than five multi-agent baselines; in a GPT-4o-mini ablation, Laya’s coordination decisions scored 84.17% against 82.34% for random choices from the same legal menus and 83.14% for a GPT controller that used about four times as many tokens.
claims.metric: GPT-4o token reduction against multi-agent baselines (minimum)
limitations: Three seeds; tokens and latency include every GPT call.
claims.headline: Laya coordinates agents with 78–94% fewer GPT tokens; random choices trail by 1.8 points

claims.subject: arxiv:2610.08775
claims.claim_text: Against zero-shot Jev (jev-1.13.0) on 1,000-item samples, an Opus 5 agent’s bottled solution reached macro-F1 0.499 on ESCI against Jev’s 0.531 at about a quarter of Jev’s projected full-workload cost ($26.28 against $104.89), and a Gemini 3.1 Pro solution reached AUROC 0.822 on RAID against 0.846 at about 2% of the cost ($4.69 against $223.16); Jev’s cost grows with workload size, whereas a bottled artifact is reused.
claims.metric: projected full-workload cost relative to Jev (ESCI)
limitations: Jev evaluated on 1,000-item samples; costs projected.
claims.headline: Agent-built artifacts: 94–97% of Jev’s quality at 2–25% of its projected cost
